strategy.angle: Energy-compute independence as a competitive moat for modern business
strategy.audience: Houston business leaders, energy executives, and tech stakeholders

draft.hook: The biggest threat to AI adoption isn't technical debt—it’s the grid.
draft.body:
The smartest move in the AI race isn't acquiring more GPUs; it’s securing exclusive control over the electrons needed to run them. OpenAI’s Stargate project with Sur Energy marks a tectonic shift: we are moving away from grid-dependent data centers toward 'energy-as-a-service.' By decoupling compute growth from urban power infrastructure, they’ve created a blueprint that bypasses the capacity bottlenecks currently paralyzing expansion.

Why does this matter to the Houston energy corridor? Because the next generation of industrial AI will be won by those who treat power generation as a core business function, not a utility bill. We are seeing a 40% projected increase in data center power demand by 2030, and the grid simply cannot keep pace. 

How do local firms respond to this shifting landscape? They stop viewing their energy providers as passive suppliers and start negotiating as infrastructure partners. At Amplify Intelligence, when I work with clients, we focus on the intersection of energy resilience and machine learning deployment; if your AI strategy doesn't account for energy autonomy, your competitive advantage will erode the moment grid prices spike. Leon Coe and the team here are already scouting these decentralized architectures for regional players.
draft.closing: Energy independence is the new operational edge. Your AI strategy is only as powerful as the source that keeps it running.
draft.cta: If you aren't auditing your energy footprint alongside your GPU roadmap, where exactly do you plan to draw power from in 2026?
